title: Sharding
subtitle: Split one huge table across machines, then watch hot keys, scatter-gather queries and resharding test the design.
learn: How range and hash partitioning place rows, and what each makes easy or hard
What makes a good shard key, and why it must appear in your hot queries
Why hot partitions happen even with hashing, and how to relieve them
What a cross-shard query costs and why tail latency grows with fan-out
How resharding moves data, and why fixed buckets beat hash mod N

steps.title: One database is not enough
steps.body: Picture an orders table with 300 million rows, about 6 TB, taking 20,000 writes per second at peak. One machine runs out of disk, memory and write throughput. Read replicas help reads, but each copy still holds all 6 TB and every write still hits one leader. Sharding splits the rows themselves: here three shards hold about 2 TB and 6,700 writes per second each.
steps.idea: Replication copies the whole dataset; sharding divides it so each machine owns only a slice.
steps.caption: Three shards, each owning about a third of the rows.

steps.title: Route by shard key
steps.body: Every row carries a shard key, here user_id. A router looks the key up in a shard map and sends the query to the one shard that owns it. The app never needs to know how many shards exist. The map is tiny, so routers cache it and refresh it only when it changes.
steps.idea: The shard key decides where a row lives, so every query is routed by it.
steps.caption: User 8841 is routed to Shard B and nowhere else.

steps.title: Hash partitioning spreads load
steps.body: With hash partitioning the shard is chosen from hash(user_id), so neighbouring ids land on unrelated shards. Inserts and reads spread almost evenly across all three. The price is order: a range scan such as user ids 1000 to 2000 now touches every shard, because adjacent keys are deliberately scattered.
steps.idea: Hashing buys even spread by giving up range scans on the key.
steps.caption: Writes fan out evenly across A, B and C.

steps.title: Range partitioning keeps order
steps.body: Range partitioning gives each shard a contiguous slice of keys, for example order dates by month. Scanning one month, or the newest 100 orders, hits one shard and is cheap. But if the key is a timestamp, every new insert lands in the newest range. That one shard takes nearly all the writes while the older shards sit almost idle.
steps.idea: Ranges make scans cheap but concentrate writes whenever the key grows over time.
steps.caption: Today's writes all pile onto the newest range, Shard C.

steps.title: Choosing the shard key
steps.body: A good key has many distinct values, spreads traffic evenly, and appears in your most common queries. Sharding orders by user_id makes the query show me my orders hit exactly one shard. Sharding by country would give only about 200 values, wildly uneven sizes, and a few giant shards. Pick the key from your access pattern, not from the schema.
steps.idea: Pick a high-cardinality key that your hottest queries already filter on.
steps.caption: A query that carries the key touches one shard.

steps.title: A hot partition
steps.body: Now one tenant, say a viral store, generates 40 percent of all traffic. Hashing cannot help: every request carries the same key, so they all land on the same shard. That shard saturates while the others idle. Fixes include a cache in front, giving the big tenant a dedicated shard, or splitting its key with a small suffix so its rows spread over several shards.
steps.idea: Hashing spreads different keys evenly, but it cannot spread one key that is itself hot.
steps.caption: One hot key overloads Shard A while B and C coast.

steps.title: A query without the key
steps.body: Someone asks for all orders from merchant 77. The merchant is not the shard key, so the router cannot tell which shard holds them. It sends the query to every shard and merges the answers, called scatter-gather. The result is only as fast as the slowest shard. Cross-shard joins and transactions are harder still, so design schemas to avoid them.
steps.idea: A query missing the shard key fans out to every shard, and the slowest shard sets the latency.
steps.caption: The router asks all three shards and waits for the last reply.

steps.title: Resharding: add a fourth shard
steps.body: Growth means adding Shard D. With plain hash mod N, going from 3 to 4 shards changes the owner of about 75 percent of keys, which is a huge copy. The standard fix is many fixed buckets, say 256, mapped to shards by the shard map. Adding D moves only whole buckets, roughly one quarter of the data, taken evenly from A, B and C.
steps.idea: Hash into fixed buckets and move buckets, so a new shard takes only its fair share of the data.
steps.caption: A, B and C each hand some buckets to D.

steps.title: Switching over safely
steps.body: Live traffic keeps writing while buckets copy. The usual pattern is: bulk copy, replay the changes made during the copy until D is almost caught up, briefly pause writes to those buckets, then update the shard map so the router points them at D. Old copies are deleted later. Clients see at most a short blip, never a stop.
steps.idea: Copy, catch up, flip the map, then clean up; the map change is the moment ownership moves.
steps.caption: The router receives a new shard map and routes to D.

steps.title: What to remember
steps.body: Sharding splits rows across machines by a shard key. Hash partitioning spreads load but loses range scans; range partitioning keeps order but can create a hot newest shard. Pick a key that is high-cardinality and present in your main queries. Expect hot keys and scatter-gather as costs, and reshard by moving fixed buckets. Shard last: indexes, caching and replicas are cheaper first.
steps.idea: Shard only when one machine truly cannot cope, and choose the key for your queries.
steps.caption: Four shards, one router, one map.

quiz.q: A cluster uses hash(key) mod N to pick a shard and grows from 3 to 4 shards. About what share of keys change owner?
quiz.why: Only keys whose value mod 3 equals mod 4 stay put, about one in four. The rest move, which is why fixed buckets in a shard map are preferred.

quiz.q: Orders are range-partitioned by created_at. Write latency spikes on exactly one shard at peak while the others are idle. What is the cause?
options: Every new order falls in the newest range, so that shard takes all inserts
The shard map is out of date
quiz.why: A monotonically increasing key sends all fresh writes to the last range. A hashed key, or a compound key that leads with something well spread, avoids it.

quiz.q: A multi-tenant app shards by tenant_id with hashing, but one tenant sends 40 percent of traffic and its shard is overloaded. What best addresses it?
options: Add more shards to the cluster
Switch from hash to range partitioning
Hash the tenant_id with a stronger function
Give that tenant its own shard, or split its key with a suffix across several shards
quiz.why: All of one tenant's requests share one key, so any hash maps them to the same shard. More shards or a better hash cannot split a single key; you must change how that key is placed.

quiz.q: In an 8-shard cluster you query by a column that is not the shard key. What happens, and what limits the latency?
options: The router guesses one shard and may miss rows
It scatters to all 8 shards, and the slowest shard sets the latency
It scans only the shard that was most recently used
It fails, because non-key queries are not allowed
quiz.why: Without the key the router cannot narrow the target, so it queries every shard and merges. The query waits for the slowest reply, so the chance of hitting one slow shard grows with fan-out.

cheatsheet.def: The column(s) whose value decides which shard owns a row. Choose high cardinality, even spread, and presence in your hot queries.
Shard = hash(key) mapped to a bucket. Spreads load evenly, but adjacent keys are scattered, so range scans hit every shard.
Each shard owns a contiguous key range. Great for range scans; risks hot shards when keys grow over time, like timestamps.
One shard receiving far more traffic than its peers, often due to a single popular key. Fix with caching, key splitting or a dedicated shard.
Sending a query to all shards and merging results. Latency is the slowest shard's, and cost grows with shard count.
Hash into many logical buckets (for example 256) and map buckets to shards. Resharding moves whole buckets instead of rehashing every key.
Small lookup table of which shard owns which bucket or range. Routers cache it; updating it is the cutover moment in resharding.
Shard last. Try indexes, caching, read replicas and a bigger machine first, since sharding permanently complicates joins and transactions.
